name: Cerebellum
func: Coordinates movement, balance and posture, and fine-tunes the timing and accuracy of every movement. It also helps with motor learning, like getting better at a skill with practice.

levels.kid:
The **cerebellum** is the "little brain." It sits at the back of your head, tucked under the big brain, and it looks a bit like a wrinkly cauliflower.

It is your body's **balance and coordination coach**. When you ride a bike, catch a ball or walk along a curb without falling, your cerebellum is busy making tiny fixes so your moves are smooth and land in the right spot.

It also helps you **learn** moves. The first time you try to skip, it is wobbly. After lots of practice, your cerebellum has learned the move, so it feels easy.
levels.hs:
The **cerebellum** sits in the back of the skull, in the **posterior cranial fossa**, below the **occipital lobes** and separated from them by a sheet of dura called the **tentorium cerebelli**. It lies behind the **pons** and **medulla**, with the **fourth ventricle** in between. Three pairs of stalks, the **cerebellar peduncles** (superior, middle and inferior), connect it to the brainstem.

It has two **hemispheres** joined by a narrow middle strip called the **vermis**. Its surface is folded into thin ridges called **folia**. It makes up only about 10% of the brain's volume, yet it contains **more than half of all the brain's neurons**, mostly tiny **granule cells**.

The cerebellum does not start movements. Instead, it compares what you **intended** to do with what your body is **actually** doing, using signals from muscles, joints, the inner ear and eyes, and then it corrects errors in real time.

One unusual rule: each cerebellar hemisphere controls the **same side** of the body. Damage on the right makes the right arm and leg clumsy.
levels.college:
The cerebellum is divided in two ways.

**Anatomically**, the **primary fissure** separates the **anterior lobe** from the **posterior lobe**, and the **posterolateral fissure** separates the **flocculonodular lobe**.

**Functionally**, there are three zones:
- **Vestibulocerebellum** (flocculonodular lobe): balance and eye movements; it connects with the vestibular nuclei.
- **Spinocerebellum** (vermis and the paravermal intermediate zone): posture, gait and limb movement corrections, using spinal input; outputs through the **fastigial** and **interposed** (globose and emboliform) nuclei.
- **Cerebrocerebellum** (lateral hemispheres): planning and timing of skilled movements; output from the **dentate nucleus** to the thalamus and motor cortex.

The cortex has three layers: the **molecular layer**, the **Purkinje cell layer**, and the **granular layer**. Inputs arrive as **mossy fibers** (from the pontine nuclei, spinal cord and vestibular system) and **climbing fibers** (only from the **inferior olive**). The only output of the cortex is the **Purkinje cells**, which are inhibitory (GABA) and project to the **deep cerebellar nuclei**.

Peduncles: the **middle** carries input from the pons; the **inferior** carries spinal and olivary input; the **superior** carries most output. Blood supply comes from the **SCA**, **AICA** and **PICA**.
levels.phd:
The cerebellar microcircuit is a classic model in neuroscience. Each **Purkinje cell** has a flat, fan-shaped dendritic tree crossed by up to roughly 200,000 **parallel fibers** (granule cell axons), but it receives input from just **one climbing fiber**, which wraps its dendrites with hundreds of synapses. A climbing fiber input triggers a **complex spike**, a burst with a large dendritic calcium signal, while parallel fiber input drives ordinary **simple spikes**.

The **Marr–Albus–Ito** theory proposes that climbing fibers carry an **error signal** that teaches the circuit. When parallel fiber and climbing fiber activity coincide, the parallel fiber synapses weaken through **long-term depression (LTD)**, which depends on mGluR1, calcium and AMPA receptor internalization. Plasticity at other sites (parallel fiber LTP, interneuron and deep nuclear synapses) also contributes. Classic models are **eyeblink conditioning** and adaptation of the **vestibulo-ocular reflex**.

Interneurons shape the signal: **basket** and **stellate cells** inhibit Purkinje cells, while **Golgi cells** provide feedback inhibition to granule cells. The granular layer is thought to perform **expansion recoding**, turning mossy fiber input into sparse, high-dimensional patterns.

Purkinje cells are organized into parasagittal **zebrin II (aldolase C)** stripes that differ in firing rate and plasticity. The cerebellum also contributes to cognition and emotion through closed loops with prefrontal and parietal cortex; the **cerebellar cognitive affective syndrome** (Schmahmann) describes deficits in planning, language and affect after posterior lobe damage. The cerebellum is thought to build **internal (forward) models** that predict the sensory consequences of movement.
levels.expert:
Cerebellar signs are **ipsilateral** because the output is double-crossed. Remember **DANISH**: Dysdiadochokinesia, Ataxia, Nystagmus, Intention tremor, Slurred (scanning) speech, Hypotonia.

Bedside tests: **finger–nose** (intention tremor, dysmetria), **heel–shin**, **rapid alternating movements**, tandem gait and the **rebound** phenomenon. Romberg is usually **negative** in cerebellar disease, which helps separate it from sensory ataxia. **Midline (vermis)** lesions give truncal and gait ataxia with relatively normal limbs; **hemispheric** lesions give limb ataxia.

**Cerebellar stroke and hemorrhage** are emergencies: swelling in the tight posterior fossa can compress the brainstem and block the fourth ventricle, causing **obstructive hydrocephalus**. Large infarcts or hematomas (classically more than about 3 cm with deterioration) may need **suboccipital decompressive craniectomy** and an external ventricular drain. Isolated acute vertigo can be cerebellar rather than inner ear; the **HINTS** exam helps tell them apart.

Children's posterior fossa tumors are core neurosurgery: **medulloblastoma** (the most common malignant pediatric brain tumor, often arising from the vermis), **pilocytic astrocytoma** (cyst with an enhancing mural nodule, excellent prognosis if fully removed) and **ependymoma**. After vermis surgery some children develop **cerebellar mutism syndrome**, usually temporary.

Other conditions: **Chiari malformation** (tonsillar descent), **Dandy–Walker malformation** (cystic fourth ventricle with vermis hypoplasia), **spinocerebellar ataxias** and **Friedreich ataxia** (inherited), and **paraneoplastic cerebellar degeneration** with anti-Yo antibodies. MRI is the imaging of choice because CT is degraded by bone artifact in the posterior fossa.

keyPoints: Sits behind the brainstem under the occipital lobes, below the tentorium
Coordinates movement; damage → ataxia on the SAME side
Purkinje cells are the only (inhibitory) output of the cortex
Mossy fibers and climbing fibers (from the inferior olive) are its two inputs
Posterior fossa swelling can cause hydrocephalus and brainstem compression

test.q: A lesion of the right cerebellar hemisphere causes clumsiness on which side?
test.explain: Cerebellar output is double-crossed, so cerebellar signs are ipsilateral.

test.q: The large output cells of the cerebellar cortex are called ______ cells.
test.explain: Purkinje cells are the only output of the cerebellar cortex and they are inhibitory (GABA).

test.q: Climbing fibers come only from the:
test.explain: Each Purkinje cell gets one climbing fiber, which originates in the inferior olivary nucleus.

test.q: Which functional zone controls balance and eye movements?
test.explain: The flocculonodular lobe connects with the vestibular nuclei to control balance and gaze.

test.q: Inability to perform rapid alternating movements is called ______.
test.explain: It is a classic cerebellar sign, the D in DANISH.
